title: Why Chasing Perfection Slowed Me Down (and What I Did Instead)
description: A personal reflection on how perfectionism held me back and how shifting focus to progress helped me grow.
body:
I used to think perfection was the goal. Every time I started something new—whether it was writing, coding, or even something as small as organizing my desk—I’d imagine the end result being flawless. That sounds like a good mindset, right? Except it wasn’t.

The problem was that aiming for perfection didn’t push me forward. It froze me in place. I’d delay starting because I wasn’t “ready.” I’d scrap drafts halfway through because they didn’t feel good enough. I’d waste hours tweaking the smallest details while ignoring the big picture. Instead of making progress, I was stuck in an endless loop of almost-finished things.

The turning point came when I realized that perfection was an illusion. No matter how much effort I put in, I’d always find something to “fix.” The more I chased it, the further it ran away.

So I decided to flip the script. Instead of chasing perfection, I started chasing progress. Here’s what I changed:

1. First drafts are allowed to be ugly. My new rule was simple: done is better than perfect. Even if my first version was rough, at least it existed.  
2. Progress over polish. I gave myself permission to focus on finishing the main thing before obsessing over details.  
3. Feedback beats assumptions. Instead of hiding my work until it was “perfect,” I started sharing earlier. Getting real feedback helped me more than endless polishing ever could.

Once I made this shift, I noticed something surprising. The more I focused on progress, the more consistent I became. And funny enough, my results improved too. Imperfect work done consistently turned out to be way more impactful than perfect work that never left my head.

Takeaway: Chasing perfection slowed me down because I was chasing something that didn’t exist. Progress, on the other hand, is real and achievable. If you keep moving forward, you’ll get better naturally—and that’s far more valuable than waiting for perfect.

title: The Time I Burned Out Trying to Do Everything at Once
description: A story about how doing less but focusing on persistence taught me more than trying to do everything at once.
body:
There was a phase in my life when I thought the key to success was doing it all. My days were jam-packed—coding projects, workouts, reading goals, side hustles, even “relaxation” was scheduled. On paper, it looked like discipline. In reality, I was exhausting myself.

TThe mistake I made was simple: I confused being busy with being effective. II believed that the more I did, the faster I’d grow.

I remember one evening sitting at my desk, staring at a bloated to-do list, and realizing I couldn’t even start. My energy was gone. My brain refused to cooperate. That night, I felt something snap: what’s the point of consistency if I’m consistently running myself into the ground?

That was the turning point.

I began to see that it wasn’t just about being consistent—it was about being persistent with the right things. Consistency is showing up, but persistence is staying with what matters, even when it’s tough. And the truth was, half the things on my list didn’t matter.

Here’s how I shifted:

1. Cutting the noise. I dropped the “busywork” tasks and focused only on the ones that truly moved me closer to my goals.  
2. Persistence over perfection. Instead of spreading thin across ten projects, I stuck with fewer but made sure I didn’t quit when it got boring or difficult.  
3. Redefining growth. I stopped chasing the image of a packed calendar and started chasing depth—how deeply I could learn, create, or enjoy something.

Ironically, by doing less, I achieved more. The projects I stuck with grew stronger. The habits I kept became solid. I felt less like I was sprinting in circles and more like I was walking a steady path forward.

Takeaway: Burnout taught me that consistency alone isn’t the magic—it’s persistence with what actually matters. Doing less, but refusing to give up on the important things, created more growth than all my “do everything” days ever did.

title: How I Found Out My Way of Learning
description: A reflection on discovering my own learning style by moving away from cramming and building habits that work for me.
body:
For the longest time, I believed that learning was about cramming as much as possible into a single day. I’d sit for hours, forcing myself to cover everything at once—tutorials, notes, new concepts—hoping the intensity would translate into results. Sometimes it worked in the short term, but most of the time, it left me drained and frustrated. I was “learning,” but not in a way that felt right for me.

The turning point came when I started asking myself a simple question after each study session: what actually worked today? Instead of just tracking how much I finished, I reflected on how I felt. Was I focused? Did I enjoy the process? Did something actually stick? That small bit of reflection changed everything.

Slowly, I noticed patterns. On days I broke tasks into smaller chunks, I remembered more. When I planned ahead instead of cramming, I felt less anxious. Writing down my own thoughts about a concept made it stick far better than copying someone else’s notes. The difference wasn’t about how much time I spent, but about how I spent it.

Here’s what I figured out about myself:

1. Structure beats chaos. A simple plan with clear steps worked better than endless hours of “winging it.”  
2. Reflection builds retention. Taking five minutes to jot down what I learned in my own words made knowledge feel mine.  
3. Energy matters. The quality of my learning was tied to how I felt—tired, distracted, or inspired. Respecting that rhythm improved my sessions.

Over time, I realized I wasn’t just learning coding or any subject—I was learning how I learn best. That shift felt powerful. I stopped trying to fit into someone else’s system and built my own. Now, instead of cramming everything into a single day, I follow a pace that feels sustainable and rewarding.

Takeaway: Real growth isn’t just about what you learn—it’s about learning how you learn. Once I understood my own habits and rhythms, I went from cramming and burning out to building a system that actually works for me. That discovery made learning feel less like a grind and more like progress.
